analysis.one_liner: Stops the handover of a sacred tribal site, Oak Flat, to a mining company.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee on March 23, 2021 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2015 defense bill required the Forest Service to hand over 2,422 acres of Tonto National Forest known as Oak Flat to Resolution Copper Mining, a company planning one of the largest copper mines in the country. The Save Oak Flat Act would repeal that land transfer and permanently withdraw Oak Flat from mining claims and disposal, keeping the land in public hands. Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site for Apache and other tribes, and the mine's planned method would cause the surface to collapse. Sanders introduced the bill with 7 Democratic cosponsors; the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribes that hold ceremonies at Oak Flat, including the San Carlos Apache, keep access to a site their religions depend on. Nearby communities avoid the risks of a mine that would remove a cubic mile of ore from 7,000 feet underground, causing the surface to subside and drawing down and potentially polluting groundwater in a desert region. The public keeps the land and the wildlife and recreation values it supports.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that the Forest Service convey Oak Flat to Resolution Copper Mining in exchange for the company's parcels of land [S2][S3].
Withdraws Oak Flat from all entry, disposal, mining claims, and mineral and geothermal leasing, so no future land transfer or mining claim could take it without new legislation [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state Resolution Copper plans block cave mining that will collapse the surface and destroy the sacred areas listed in the National Register of Historic Places, and that the conveyance was mandated regardless of the outcome of environmental review or tribal consultation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper, the mining venture behind the proposed mine, loses its congressionally granted land transfer and the ore beneath it. Copper consumers and the domestic copper supply would not gain that new source of production; southern Arizona governments and businesses expecting mine-related jobs and revenue would not see them.

drawbacks.text: Copper is essential for electrical wiring, wind turbines, and electric vehicles, and Resolution Copper's deposit is estimated to be one of the largest in the United States; blocking the mine forfeits domestic copper supply and the jobs and tax base a large mine would bring to Pinal County, Arizona [S3].

The land exchange was written into the 2015 defense authorization law, so Resolution Copper has a statutory entitlement and investors relied on it; repealing it raises the question of whether Congress should reverse a completed legislative bargain [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on one mining project and the copper supply and jobs it would have produced; the benefit is permanent protection of a tribal sacred site and groundwater in an arid region. The original transfer was designed to run regardless of environmental review, so repeal was the only way to stop it. A fairer path might have been requiring the environmental review to genuinely gate the transfer, but this bill chose outright repeal, which was its stated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, with 7 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, whose jurisdiction covers public lands [S5].
No further action was ever taken; no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote appears in the action history, and the bill expired at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Resolution Copper is better off: the 2015 land-transfer mandate stayed on the books, the Forest Service continued moving toward publishing the environmental review that triggers the transfer, and no senator ever had to vote on record. The committee chair and members who let it sit never had to take a position either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Resolution Copper and the mine's backers

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Save Oak Flat Act and sponsored it.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Resolution Copper Mining, LLC
against.role: Mining venture (Rio Tinto and BHP joint venture)
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the existing 2015 land-transfer mandate and continued pursuing the transfer while repeal legislation sat unacted upon.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood; sponsorship was limited to one Independent and 7 of 48 Senate Democrats, and the Democratic chair who controlled its committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, the Rio Tinto–BHP joint venture)
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the 2015 mandate handing the company 2,422 acres of national forest land, along with roughly a cubic mile of copper ore beneath it. Because it died, the company keeps its congressionally granted entitlement to the land and the ore. The mine's planned block caving would collapse the surface of a tribal sacred site and draw on desert groundwater, so the company's gain runs against the people who use that land and water [S3].

Blocking the mine forfeits a large new domestic copper source at a time of rising demand for wiring and clean-energy hardware. This is the strongest economic argument against the bill, and it was never weighed by a committee hearing [S3].
